reason: Cupule (a FLOPO class) can have a surface texture. The examples are mostly about the wall (crustaceous), which is part of the cupule, so I accept it.
A nut can be pointed. The examples say 'apex pointed', so the apex is the true bearer where the apex is named. The pair itself is fine.
Hastate anthers (arrow-shaped at the base) are normal in several families.
Stalks, here fern stipes, are described as robust or sturdy.
An involucre or cupule can be cleft, and the examples agree.
Enlarged nodes are a standard stem character (grasses, Polygonaceae).
A leaf sheath can taper to an attenuate apex. The examples are correct.
Fan-shaped (flabellate) leaf blades are normal, for example in palms.
A perianth can be bowl-shaped or crateriform.
Stamens and filaments can be robust. Some examples describe a spur, but most are about the stamen.
A perianth tube can be pubescent, and the examples agree.
A leaf sinus can be semicircular, as in the examples.
The margin of a leaflet blade can be crenate. This is the usual rule that the margin shape goes to the blade.
Petals can be setose, so the pair is botanically fine. The 'with a 1-3-setose tip' example is a count, not a quality.
The orchid column (gynostemium) can be suberect, and the examples are correct.

'Spatial pattern' is a generic attribute. The examples mix a shape (complanate), a surface pattern (reticulate) and a dotting (gland-dotted). A rule would need to map each word to its own specific term and drop the generic attribute.
A corolla lip or its lobe can be subelliptic, and the examples agree.
A short leaf rachis is a normal character (palms, ferns).
Bracts can be lobate, and the examples agree.
Sepals can be coloured (petaloid) instead of green. The quality is vague but valid.
Fern sporangia can be hairy. One example describes glands on stalks, which is a different thing, but the pair is fine.
A corolla lip can be oblanceolate.
A megasporophyll (for example in cycads) can be hairy or glabrescent. The generic attribute is acceptable here.
There is only one bare 'glabrous' with no context, most likely the ovary or another part wrongly read as the ovule. Ovules are normally not hairy, so the pair arises from a wrong reading.
The gynostemium surface can be papillate (texture), and the examples agree.
A corolla lip is often striated with lines of colour.
Adnate and connate describe how two parts are joined (a relation to another part), not a structure quality of the corona. Handle them by the fusion pattern, not by this attribute.
A pinna can be forked, and the examples describe the pinna.
The 'subglobose' in the examples belongs to the mentum (an orchid chin made by the sepals), not to the sepal. A rule would need a separate mentum bearer and must not move it to the sepal.
The epichile (the end part of an orchid lip) can be glabrous.
The hypochile surface can be papillose or barbellate (texture).
Lithocysts are described as conspicuous, as in Ficus, so this is plausible. The examples are short and lack context.
Veins and veinlets can be flat (level with the blade) or raised.
Veinlets can be forked (furcate), and the examples agree.
An involucel (the small outer cup in Dipsacaceae) can be toothed, and the examples agree.
A moss operculum (capsule lid) can be short.
The examples are ratios to another part ('1/3 as long as nutlet'). They are not the length of the organ base, so the part is wrong. Use the ratio pattern (pattern 10).
Glumes in grasses and sedges are fertile or sterile.
A corolla lobe margin can be erose. The margin goes to the lobe.
A moss calyptra can be fringed at the base.
Peristome parts are described as hyaline or transparent. 'Hyaline' is read as transparent.
The apex of the epichile can be emarginate.
A leaf sinus can be open or closed, and the examples agree.
An epicalyx bract or lobe can be lanceolate.

'Few capsules' or 'few fruits per infructescence' counts the fruits in a bigger structure. The fruit is not the bearer. The bearer should be the infructescence or the plant, and a count of fruits is not a quality of a single fruit.
A gland or secretory tissue can have a flat surface.
A cyathium can be stipitate or sessile.
Annual shoots (versus perennial) are a normal shoot character.
The examples are leaf veins and areoles, not vascular bundles. The pair arises from a wrong reading of the bearer, and veins already have their own class.
Moss peristome teeth can be forked.
An ovary can be laterally compressed, and the examples agree.
The apex of the hypochile can be obtuse or rounded. 'Obtuse' is the nearest PATO term for rounded.
A hypochile can be conical or subconic.
The length of a corolla plica is meaningful. The examples are bare measurements with no quality word, so the part is trusted and not checked.
'Characteristic' is a vague root term. The examples ('margin entire or denticulate') describe the margin shape, so the pair arises from a wrong reading of the quality.
A short androgynophore is a normal character (Passiflora, Capparaceae).
A petiole can have a colour, and the examples give green or brown. Some examples also list hairs, which belong to a hair pattern.
Sporangia can be visible or conspicuous on the sporophyll. The examples all describe this, but they are about visibility, so this is a weak fit.
An involucre can be small, and the examples agree.
An indusium (the cover over a fern sorus) can be medium-sized.
